title: DAVID COLLECTED WIVES LONG BEFORE BATHSHEBA ENTERED THE STORY
paragraphs: DAVID COLLECTED WIVES LONG BEFORE BATHSHEBA ENTERED THE STORY

Bathsheba was not the beginning of David’s compromise. Long before the rooftop, the secret summons, the pregnancy, and the bloodshed, Scripture had already been leaving warning signs in David’s story—and perhaps the most frightening part is how ordinary those warning signs looked.
A king walking when he should have been at war.
A loyal soldier deliberately abandoned to die.
Then a prophet standing before a throne and saying words that shattered the king’s illusion:
That is how many people remember David’s great scandal.
But what if the tragedy did not actually begin with Bathsheba?
What if 2 Samuel 11 was an explosion whose fuse had been burning for years?
Because long before David saw Bathsheba, David had already been collecting wives.
That detail matters because some of the most destructive sins in our lives do not begin on the night everything collapses.
One appetite we refuse to confront.
One thing we know is spiritually dangerous, but because lightning does not immediately fall from heaven, we begin convincing ourselves that perhaps God does not care as much as we thought.
And eventually something that once troubled our conscience becomes normal.
That may be one of the most terrifying sentences you will read today:
You can become comfortable with something that is slowly preparing you for catastrophe.
David did not wake up one morning as a murderer.
He did not begin his story as the king who took another man’s wife.
He was the shepherd boy who trusted God when grown warriors trembled.
He was the young man who looked at Goliath and saw something everybody else had forgotten: the giant was enormous, but God was greater.
He spared Saul when killing Saul could have accelerated his own promotion.
Scripture would remember him as a man after God’s own heart.
And that is precisely why his story should make believers uncomfortable.
Because spiritual history does not make anyone immune to spiritual compromise.
Yesterday’s obedience cannot substitute for today’s surrender.
You can have killed giants and still need to kill the appetite growing quietly inside you.
Before Bathsheba ever appears in David’s story, Scripture has already introduced us to multiple wives.
Michal was Saul’s daughter and David’s wife (1 Samuel 18:27).

Later, while David was living in the wilderness, we encounter Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, formerly the wife of Nabal. First Samuel 25:42–43 tells us that Abigail became David’s wife and then immediately says:
“David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel, and they both were his wives.”
Second Samuel 3:2–5 records sons born to David in Hebron through Ahinoam, Abigail, Maacah, Haggith, Abital, and Eglah.
Then comes a verse that is easy to read quickly because it does not immediately contain adultery, murder, confrontation, or judgment.
“After he left Hebron, David took more concubines and wives in Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to him.”
And all of this appears before the Bathsheba account of 2 Samuel 11.
The Bible is not hiding the trajectory.
But we must be careful here, because faithfully reading Scripture means refusing to confuse biblical description with biblical approval.
The fact that Scripture records something does not mean Scripture endorses it.
The Bible records polygamous households with devastating honesty, but the creation pattern reaches further back.
Genesis 2:24 describes the foundational marriage union: a man is joined to his wife, and they become “one flesh.”
Jesus Himself returns to this creation text when teaching about marriage.
In Matthew 19:5–6, the Greek preserves the same astonishing idea:
Jesus then declares that they are no longer two, but one flesh, and what God has joined together must not be separated.
And there was another command David, as Israel’s king, should have known.
Long before David wore the crown, Deuteronomy had warned Israel about what a king must not do.
“And he shall not multiply wives for himself…”
God connected multiplied wives with the danger of a diverted heart.
The warning was not merely about royal administration.

This does not mean every detail of David’s later sin with Bathsheba can be reduced to one cause. Scripture does not say, “David committed adultery with Bathsheba because he had multiple wives,” so neither should we.
But Scripture absolutely allows us to see a pattern of accumulating women before the catastrophic events of 2 Samuel 11.
Bathsheba was not David’s first departure from the creation pattern for marriage.
And suddenly the rooftop looks different.
But it no longer looks completely isolated.
This is where David’s ancient story begins walking uncomfortably close to ours.
Because perhaps you do not have a rooftop.
Perhaps nobody is being summoned to a palace.
Perhaps it is a private message.
An emotional attachment your spouse knows nothing about.
A flirtation you keep calling harmless.
A habit you keep deleting and reinstalling.
A resentment you have rehearsed so many times that bitterness now feels justified.
Maybe there has been no catastrophic scandal.
We often want God to rescue us from the dramatic sin while protecting the smaller compromises that trained our hearts to tolerate it.
We pray, “Lord, don’t let me fall.”
David’s story warns us that the scandal everyone eventually sees may have roots in compromises almost nobody noticed.
That should not make us obsessed with predicting everybody else’s downfall.
It should make us examine our own hearts.
What have you normalized that once bothered you?
What are you defending today that five years ago you would have called dangerous?
Because that word follows David before Bathsheba.
And appetites rarely announce when they have had enough.
And when he saw another man’s wife, what he possessed did not silence what he wanted.
That is the deception of uncontrolled desire.
It keeps promising satisfaction while enlarging its own capacity to hunger.
Second Samuel 11 tells us David saw her from the roof.
And someone answered with information that should have functioned like a wall:
“Isn’t this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite?”
That should have ended the matter.
But David sent messengers and took her.
When Uriah refused to cooperate unknowingly with David’s cover-up, David escalated.
This is another horrifying feature of unrepented sin.
Sin rarely remains satisfied with being one sin.
So manipulation gave way to murder.
David sent Uriah back to the battlefield carrying instructions that would arrange his own death.
And for a while, David appeared to have gotten away with it.
That may be one of the most dangerous moments in anyone’s spiritual life:
No prophet standing at the door.
But 2 Samuel 11 closes with a sentence more terrifying than public exposure:
“The thing David had done displeased the LORD.”
People did not have to know.
Nathan told David about a rich man with many sheep who stole the single beloved lamb of a poor man.
The king who could not clearly see his own sin could see somebody else’s sin immediately.
We can become experts at recognizing in others what we have learned to excuse in ourselves.
No pointing toward all the psalms David had written.
And here is where the Gospel begins shining through the wreckage.
“The LORD has taken away your sin. You are not going to die.”
David’s forgiveness did not erase every earthly consequence of his actions. Second Samuel records terrible consequences within his house.
Grace is not God pretending sin did not matter.
Grace is astonishing precisely because sin mattered so much.
And David’s brokenness later erupts in the prayer preserved in Psalm 51:
“Have mercy on me, O God, according to your unfailing love…”
He does not say, “But Saul was worse.”
He does not say, “Look at everything good I have done.”
Not getting caught and becoming embarrassed.
Repentance stops defending the darkness and turns toward God.
“Against you, you only, have I sinned…”
“Create in me a pure heart, O God…”
David finally understood something every sinner eventually has to understand.
Our deepest problem cannot be solved by becoming better at hiding.
And David could not create one himself.
This is where David’s story must ultimately take us beyond David.
David was Israel’s celebrated king, but David needed a greater King.
David defeated Goliath but could not ultimately defeat the sin within David.
Jesus Christ came from David’s royal line, yet where David failed, Christ remained faithful.
David took what was not his.
Jesus surrendered what was rightfully His.
David used power to serve his desire.
Jesus used His authority in perfect obedience to the Father and gave Himself for sinners.
David arranged for an innocent man to die to conceal his guilt.
Jesus, the truly innocent Man, willingly died to cover the guilt of people like David.
At Calvary, God did not shrug at human sin.
The cross tells us simultaneously that our sin is worse than our excuses admit and God’s grace is greater than our shame can imagine.
That is why the Gospel is not:
“Try harder so God might tolerate you.”
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again, and that forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered through Him.
You do not need to wait until your private compromise becomes a public catastrophe.
You do not need a Bathsheba-sized scandal before you become serious about the thing quietly pulling your heart away from God.
Maybe this article found you before the rooftop.
Before the resentment destroys the relationship.
Before the secret becomes a headline in your family.
Before the thing you keep controlling begins controlling you.
Then perhaps mercy is warning you early.
There is still time to close the door.
There is still time to confess.
There is still time to tell somebody trustworthy.
There is still time to repent.
There is still time to bring the hidden thing into the light.
And if you are reading this after everything has already collapsed, David’s story has something to say to you too.
Scandal does not have to write the final sentence.
But God did not abandon His redemptive purpose.
And generations later, another name would appear in David’s line.
Matthew opens the genealogy of Christ by calling Him “the son of David.”
Think about the grace contained in those words.
David’s ugliest chapter could not cancel God’s promise.
This does not minimize what David did.
It magnifies the God who redeems sinners.
And perhaps that is what somebody reading this desperately needs to hear.
But your scandal does not possess more saving power than the blood of Jesus.
Your shame is not stronger than His grace.
Maybe you have been hiding because you think exposure would make you unlovable.
Maybe you have spent years maintaining a Christian appearance while privately starving.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
And then you go home carrying something you hope nobody ever discovers.
David teaches us that spiritual usefulness is never permission to stop guarding the heart.
But David also teaches us that when God exposes sin, His purpose is not merely humiliation.
And the Gospel tells us where repentant sinners must ultimately run.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, be brave enough to make your response more than another scroll.
Someone else reading those words may realize they are not the only person fighting for surrender.
Not because David’s failure deserves preservation, but because the warning does.
There may come a night when compromise whispers that one more step will not matter.
Come back and remember the rooftop did not begin on the rooftop.
Not as a badge proving you have everything together.
Send it privately to the believer who has gone quiet.
Let the struggling husband read it.
Let the exhausted wife read it.
Let the young Christian fighting secret temptation read it.
Let the lukewarm believer read it.
Let the person who thinks Christianity is only for clean people read it.
Even let the unbeliever who thinks their past has made them unreachable read it.
If one person turns toward Jesus because you refused to keep truth to yourself, that share mattered.
Not because supporting this ministry makes anyone more saved.
But Christians have always used their time, resources, voices, generosity, and opportunities to help Gospel truth reach other people.
And if your desire is to glorify God, do not merely admire truth when it reaches you.
Ask what faithful response you can make with what He has entrusted to you.
For some, that may mean sharing this article publicly.
For others, praying for the ministry.
Because this world does not need another Christianity built around appearances.
It needs truth strong enough to confront us.
Grace deep enough to receive the repentant.
A cross bloody enough to remind us what sin costs.
An empty tomb powerful enough to prove that death does not get the last word.
And believers humble enough to admit:
David collected wives long before Bathsheba entered the story.

Bathsheba was not merely an isolated moment appearing from nowhere. Scripture had already shown David multiplying wives contrary to the warning given to Israel’s kings. We should not claim more causation than Scripture gives us, but neither should we ignore the trajectory Scripture places before our eyes.
But that is not where the Christian story ends.
And ultimately, from David’s broken family line came Jesus Christ—the flawless King David could never be.
The King who does not merely expose darkness but calls sinners out of it.
So before you leave this article, ask yourself the question nobody else can answer for you:
What have I been multiplying that God has been telling me to surrender?
Do not wait for the rooftop.
Do not wait until the private compromise acquires public consequences.
And grace is still calling your name.
Because sometimes the first crack in a prison is simply admitting that you have been living behind a locked door.
And remember this when shame tells you that your worst chapter has already decided your ending:
The rooftop may explain how David fell, but the cross explains why fallen people can still come home.
